title: Authentication and authorization
scopeHtml:
Scope: sessions vs JWT, OAuth2/OIDC flows, RBAC/ABAC, token refresh and revocation.

Scope: sessions vs JWT, OAuth2/OIDC flows, RBAC/ABAC, token refresh and revocation.

notes.title: Authentication vs authorization
notes.html:
Authentication (authn) answers "who are you?". Authorization (authz) answers "what are you allowed to do?". Authn happens once per login (or per token); authz happens on every request, for every resource.

Mechanism: the client proves identity (password, passkey, OTP, a signed token from a trusted party). The server turns that into an identity (user id, tenant, roles). Each later request carries a credential (cookie or bearer token); a gate reads it, rebuilds the identity, then asks a policy "can user 42 do DELETE on invoice 9?".

Worked example. 1M daily users, 20 requests each = 20M requests/day, about 230/s average. Password hashing (argon2id, about 100 ms CPU) happens only on logins: say 1M/day = 12/s, so about 1.2 CPU cores. The per-request authz check must cost microseconds, so it runs on in-memory claims, not a DB call.

Industry examples. Google separates the sign-in service (authn) from per-product permission checks (authz); AWS IAM is pure authz (policies evaluated on every API call); Stripe API keys identify the caller, and separate restricted-key scopes decide what it can do.

Decision gravity. Splitting authn from authz is cheap now and painful later. Authn provider choice (own vs Auth0/Cognito/Keycloak) is a semi one-way door: migrating password hashes needs rehash-on-login tricks.

Everyday analogy. The security desk checks your ID badge at the building door (authn); each office door then checks whether your badge opens that room (authz).

Common interview traps.

  • Using "auth" for both and then mixing them up (a 401 means not authenticated, a 403 means not allowed).
  • Checking authz only in the UI or only at the gateway; every service must enforce it.
  • Forgetting object-level checks (user 42 reading invoice of user 43: the classic IDOR bug).

notes.title: Password storage
notes.html:
Never store passwords; store a slow, salted hash. If the DB leaks, attackers must brute-force each password separately.

Mechanism: hash = argon2id(password, random_salt, params). The salt (16 bytes, unique per user) defeats rainbow tables and makes equal passwords hash differently. Slow means tunable cost: argon2id with about 64 MB memory, 3 iterations, 1 lane, about 100 ms. Fast hashes (MD5, SHA-256 alone) allow billions of guesses per second on a GPU. Alternatives: bcrypt (cost 12, 72-byte input limit), scrypt, PBKDF2 (needs 600k+ iterations; FIPS-friendly). A server-side pepper (secret in an HSM or KMS, not in the DB) adds a layer.

# argon2-cffi
from argon2 import PasswordHasher
ph = PasswordHasher(time_cost=3, memory_cost=65536, parallelism=1)
h = ph.hash("hunter2")      # stores salt and params inside the string
ph.verify(h, "hunter2")     # raises on mismatch
if ph.check_needs_rehash(h): pass  # upgrade params on next login

Worked example. At 100 ms and 64 MB per hash, a login burst of 200/s needs 20 cores and 12.8 GB RAM, and it is itself a DoS target. So rate-limit login and put hashing on a separate pool.

Industry examples. LinkedIn (2012) leaked unsalted SHA-1 hashes, and most were cracked within days. Modern guidance (OWASP) recommends argon2id first, bcrypt as fallback. Passkeys (WebAuthn) remove the password entirely.

Decision gravity. Hash params are reversible (rehash on next login). Choosing to store passwords at all is a liability you can avoid by delegating to OIDC or passkeys.

Everyday analogy. A shredder that only runs one way: you can check a shredded page matches a candidate, but never rebuild the original.

Common interview traps.

  • "Encrypt the passwords." Encryption is reversible; hashing is the right answer.
  • Hashing but forgetting a unique salt.
  • Unbounded login attempts (credential stuffing). Add rate limit, lockout with backoff, and breached-password checks.

notes.title: Sessions: server-side state
notes.html:
A session is a random ID in a cookie that points to user data stored on the server. The ID is meaningless by itself, so stealing the data is impossible without the server's store.

Mechanism: after login the server creates session_id = 128-bit random, stores {user_id, roles, created, last_seen} in Redis with a TTL, and sends Set-Cookie: sid=...; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax; Path=/. Each request: cookie, then a Redis GET, then identity. Logout = DEL sid, so revocation is instant.

# typical session settings
session:
  store: redis
  ttl_idle: 30m        # sliding
  ttl_absolute: 12h    # force re-login
  cookie: {httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: Lax}
  rotate_id_on_login: true   # stop session fixation

Worked example. 10M concurrent sessions x 1 KB = 10 GB in Redis; at 50k requests/s that is 50k GET/s, easily one Redis primary (about 100k ops/s) plus replicas; round trip about 0.5 ms.

Industry examples. Classic Rails, Django, Spring Session and most banks use server sessions because instant revocation matters. GitHub web uses cookie sessions; its API uses tokens.

Decision gravity. Easy to start with, cheap to reverse. Cost: every request needs a store hit and the store is a critical dependency. Breaks with multi-region (session store latency) and with mobile or third-party API clients (cookies are awkward).

Everyday analogy. A cloakroom ticket: the number means nothing alone; the attendant looks up your coat.

Common interview traps.

  • Sticky sessions instead of a shared store.
  • Not rotating the session id at login (session fixation).
  • Missing HttpOnly (XSS steals the cookie) or Secure.

notes.title: JWT: stateless tokens
notes.html:
A JWT is a signed JSON blob the client carries; the server verifies the signature instead of looking anything up. Format: base64url(header).base64url(payload).signature.

Mechanism: payload (claims) like {"sub":"u42","roles":["admin"],"iss":"https://auth.acme.com","aud":"orders-api","exp":1760000900}. The signature is HS256 (shared secret) or RS256 / ES256 (private key signs, public key verifies; services fetch keys from a JWKS URL and cache them by kid). Verification is about 50 microseconds CPU, zero network. The payload is encoded, not encrypted: anyone can read it. Never put secrets in it. Always check exp, iss, aud, and pin the algorithm (reject alg: none and HS/RS confusion).

eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsImtpZCI6ImsxIn0 . eyJzdWIiOiJ1NDIiLCJleHAiOjE3NjAwMDA5MDB9 . <sig>
 header (alg, kid)                      payload (claims)                           RSA sig

Worked example. 100 microservices at 200k requests/s total: with sessions that is 200k Redis lookups/s; with JWT it is 0 network calls, only CPU. A token with 10 claims is about 600 bytes, sent on every request: 200k x 600 B = 120 MB/s of header overhead. Keep tokens small.

Industry examples. Auth0, Okta, Cognito, Google ID tokens and Keycloak issue JWTs; Kubernetes service account tokens are JWTs; Netflix passes signed identity tokens between internal services.

Decision gravity. Stateless verification scales trivially but you cannot revoke a JWT before expiry without adding state back (see revocation). Choosing long-lived JWTs as sessions is a common one-way mistake. Use short lived (5 to 15 min) access tokens.

Everyday analogy. A signed concert wristband: staff just look at the stamp, no list lookup. But if you lose it, anyone can wear it until the show ends.

Common interview traps.

  • "JWT is encrypted." It is signed. (JWE is the encrypted variant, rarely used.)
  • Storing JWTs in localStorage (XSS reads it). Prefer an HttpOnly cookie or memory.
  • Accepting the alg from the token header without pinning.
  • Putting permissions that change often (roles) in a long-lived token; they go stale.

notes.title: Sessions vs JWT: choosing
notes.html:
Pick sessions for browser apps that need instant logout; pick short JWTs for service-to-service and mobile APIs; many real systems use both.

Server session JWT
Per-request cost Store lookup (0.5 ms) CPU verify (0.05 ms)
Revoke Instant (DEL) Wait for expiry or keep a denylist
Size on wire about 32 B cookie 400 to 1500 B
Cross-service Needs shared store Works anywhere with public key
Stale data Never (read live) Until expiry
Mobile / third party Awkward Natural

Industry examples. Hybrid is the norm: Google and Spotify issue short access tokens and long refresh tokens. Banking web apps stay on cookies. Gateways like Kong or Envoy validate JWT at the edge and pass trusted headers inward.

Decision gravity. Reversible at the edge (gateway swap) but hard to retrofit into 50 services that parse tokens themselves. Centralise verification in one library or the gateway.

Everyday analogy. Hotel key card (JWT, works until expiry offline) versus front desk looking up your name each time (session).

Common interview traps.

  • Declaring JWT "better". It is a trade: scalability vs revocation.
  • Forgetting that a JWT denylist is just a session store in disguise.

notes.title: OAuth 2.0: delegated access
notes.html:
OAuth2 lets an app act on your behalf at another service without ever seeing your password. It is about authorization (delegation), not login.

Roles: resource owner (you), client (the app), authorization server (issues tokens), resource server (the API). Mechanism: the client sends you to the authorization server, you consent to scopes (photos.read), the server returns a code, the client exchanges it for an access token, and calls the API with Authorization: Bearer <token>.

Grant types today: Authorization Code + PKCE (web, mobile, SPA: the default), Client Credentials (machine to machine, no user), Device Code (TVs, CLIs). Implicit and Password grants are deprecated (OAuth 2.1 drops them). PKCE: client sends code_challenge = SHA256(code_verifier) first, then proves the code_verifier when exchanging the code, so a stolen code is useless.

# step 1: browser redirect
GET https://auth.acme.com/authorize?response_type=code&client_id=app1
  &redirect_uri=https://app.acme.com/cb&scope=openid%20photos.read
  &state=xyz&code_challenge=E9Mel...&code_challenge_method=S256
# step 2: back-channel exchange
curl -X POST https://auth.acme.com/token \
  -d grant_type=authorization_code -d code=SplxlOBe \
  -d code_verifier=dBjftJeZ... -d client_id=app1 -d redirect_uri=https://app.acme.com/cb

Worked example. A "Sign in with Google then read Calendar" app: access token TTL 1 h, refresh token 6 months, scope calendar.readonly. If compromised, damage is limited to read-only calendar for 1 h.

Industry examples. Google, GitHub, Slack, Spotify and Stripe Connect all use OAuth2. Keycloak and Auth0 implement the server side.

Decision gravity. Scopes designed too coarse ("all") are very hard to narrow later because clients are already deployed. Design scopes per resource and action from day one.

Everyday analogy. A valet key: it starts the car and parks it, but does not open the glovebox or trunk, and you never handed over your master key.

Common interview traps.

  • Using OAuth2 alone as "login" (needs OIDC).
  • Skipping state (CSRF) or exact redirect_uri matching (open redirect, code theft).
  • Using Implicit flow for SPAs.

notes.title: OpenID Connect (OIDC)
notes.html:
OIDC is a thin identity layer on top of OAuth2 that adds an ID token, so the app learns who logged in.

Mechanism: ask for scope openid (plus profile, email). The token response also contains an ID token, a JWT with sub, iss, aud, exp, nonce and optional email. The client validates signature (keys from /.well-known/jwks.json found via /.well-known/openid-configuration), checks aud = own client id and nonce matches. A /userinfo endpoint returns more claims. ID token is for the client; the access token is for the API (do not send an ID token to APIs).

Worked example. Company SSO: employees log in once at Okta (IdP, TTL 8 h); 50 internal apps each redirect to Okta, get an ID token silently, and mint their own local session. One MFA prompt, 50 apps.

Industry examples. "Sign in with Google/Apple/Microsoft" is OIDC; Okta, Azure AD/Entra, Keycloak. SAML is the older XML cousin in enterprise SSO.

Decision gravity. Delegating login to an IdP is a good, mostly reversible choice (keep your own user id, map sub to it; do not key users by email only). Without that mapping, switching providers is a one-way pain.

Everyday analogy. Showing a passport (ID token) issued by a trusted government to a hotel, instead of the hotel inventing its own ID card.

Common interview traps.

  • Confusing ID token and access token.
  • Not validating aud, iss, exp, nonce.
  • Using email as the immutable key (emails change; use iss + sub).

notes.title: Token refresh and rotation
notes.html:
Short access tokens limit damage; a long-lived refresh token silently gets new ones. This gives JWT scalability with a revocation handle.

Mechanism: access token 5 to 15 min; refresh token 7 to 90 days, opaque and stored hashed in the DB. Client calls POST /token grant_type=refresh_token. With refresh token rotation, each use returns a new refresh token and invalidates the old one. If an old one is replayed (theft), the server detects reuse and revokes the whole token family.

t=0   access A1 (10m) + refresh R1
t=10m A1 expired -> use R1 -> get A2 + R2 (R1 dead)
attacker replays R1 -> reuse detected -> revoke family {R1,R2}, force login

Worked example. 1M mobile users, access TTL 10 min: each active user refreshes 6 times/h; 1M x 6 / 3600 = about 1,700 refresh calls/s at peak all-active, each one DB read plus write. Size the refresh store for that, and add jitter so clients do not all refresh at once.

Industry examples. Auth0 and Okta offer rotation with reuse detection; Google's OAuth refresh tokens are long-lived and revocable from the account page.

Decision gravity. TTL choice is a reversible tuning knob (security vs load). Storing refresh tokens only on the server side as hashes is cheap now and costly to retrofit.

Everyday analogy. A day pass (access) that expires each hour, renewed at the desk with your membership card (refresh). If the desk sees the same card used twice from two places, it cancels the membership.

Common interview traps.

  • Storing refresh tokens in plaintext or in localStorage.
  • Race: two tabs refreshing at once trip reuse detection. Add a short grace window or a single-flight lock client-side.

notes.title: Revocation and logout
notes.html:
Revoking means making a still-valid credential stop working now. Sessions get it free; JWTs need an extra mechanism.

Options, from cheap to strong:

  1. Short TTL only: accept up to 10 min of stale access. Zero infrastructure.
  2. Denylist of jti or sub + issued-at: gateway checks a Redis set; entries expire when the token would. Tiny: 10k revoked tokens x 40 B = 400 KB.
  3. Per-user "tokens valid after" timestamp: one value per user; reject any token with iat before it. Great for "log out everywhere" and password change.
  4. Token introspection (RFC 7662): API asks the auth server "is this active?". Strong, but a network hop each time (cache 30 s).

Worked example. Employee fired at 10:00 with a 15-min access token: set valid_after[user]=10:00, gateway rejects all tokens older than that within seconds, refresh tokens are deleted in the DB. Damage window: seconds, not 15 min.

Industry examples. Google logs you out of all sessions on password change; AWS STS temporary credentials just expire (15 min to 12 h), and IAM policy denies can still apply instantly via policy evaluation.

Decision gravity. Picking pure stateless with no revoke path is a one-way door for compliance (SOC 2 and banks require quick revocation). Add the valid_after check early; it is almost free.

Everyday analogy. Cancelling a lost credit card: either wait for it to expire (short TTL), or the bank keeps a blocked list that shops check.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "just delete the JWT on the client". The attacker still holds a copy.
  • Denylisting every token forever; entries must expire with the token.

notes.title: RBAC: role-based access control
notes.html:
RBAC gives users roles; roles carry permissions. You check "has role X" instead of per-user lists.

Mechanism: tables users, roles, permissions, user_roles, role_permissions. Example roles: viewer, editor, admin. Permission strings like invoice:read, invoice:delete. Check in code: if (!user.can("invoice:delete")) 403. Add hierarchy (admin includes editor) and scoping (role per tenant or project: Alice is admin in project A, viewer in B).

CREATE TABLE user_roles (user_id BIGINT, role_id INT, scope_type TEXT, scope_id BIGINT,
  PRIMARY KEY (user_id, role_id, scope_type, scope_id));
-- can alice delete invoices in project 7?
SELECT 1 FROM user_roles ur JOIN role_permissions rp USING (role_id)
WHERE ur.user_id=1 AND rp.permission='invoice:delete'
  AND ur.scope_type='project' AND ur.scope_id=7;

Worked example. 5,000 employees, 30 roles, 200 permissions. Managing 5,000 x 200 per-user grants is 1M rows; with roles it is 5,000 role assignments plus a 30 x 200 matrix.

Industry examples. Kubernetes RBAC (Role, RoleBinding), AWS IAM groups/roles, GitHub org roles (read, triage, write, maintain, admin).

Decision gravity. RBAC is the right default and easy to reverse. It breaks with role explosion ("editor-in-EU-for-team-blue-during-office-hours"), the signal to move to ABAC.

Everyday analogy. Job badges in an office: "Nurse" opens the pharmacy; nobody lists each nurse by name per door.

Common interview traps.

  • Checking role names in code (if role == "admin") instead of permissions; changes then need deploys.
  • Ignoring resource ownership; roles alone cannot say "only your own documents".

notes.title: ABAC and relationship-based access
notes.html:
ABAC decides using attributes of the user, the resource, the action and the context, so rules are expressive without creating a role per case.

Mechanism: policy allow if user.department == resource.department AND resource.sensitivity <= user.clearance AND time in business hours. A policy engine (OPA/Rego, AWS Cedar, XACML) evaluates it. Variant: ReBAC (relationship-based, Google Zanzibar): permissions come from a graph of tuples like doc:readme#viewer@user:alice and folder:x#parent@doc:readme, so "viewers of a folder can view its docs" is derived.

# Rego (OPA) style
allow { input.action == "read"; input.user.dept == input.doc.dept }

Worked example. Google Drive-style sharing: 10B objects, 100M checks/s planet-wide. Zanzibar answers in under 10 ms at p95 using cached relation tuples and consistency tokens ("zookies") to avoid the "new enemy" problem (revoked access then seeing old data).

Industry examples. Google Zanzibar (Drive, YouTube), open-source SpiceDB, OpenFGA (Auth0 FGA), Airbnb and Carta use similar systems; AWS IAM conditions and Cedar (Verified Permissions) are ABAC.

Decision gravity. Moving to a central policy engine is a heavy, semi one-way door: every service gets a network dependency (latency, failure mode: fail closed or open?). Do it when role explosion or sharing graphs make RBAC hopeless; start with RBAC plus ownership checks.

Everyday analogy. RBAC is "staff may enter"; ABAC is "staff of this department, with level 3 clearance, between 9 and 5, may open this folder".

Common interview traps.

  • Jumping to ABAC for a simple admin/user app.
  • Not saying whether the policy check fails open or closed (answer: closed).
  • Putting a remote policy call on the hot path without caching.

notes.title: Where to enforce and common attacks
notes.html:
Authenticate at the edge, authorize at every service. The gateway verifies the token (cheap, rejects junk early); each service still checks its own resource permissions because internal callers can bypass the gateway.

Typical flaws and fixes:

  • IDOR / BOLA (OWASP API #1): GET /invoices/43 as user 42. Fix: always scope queries (WHERE id=? AND tenant_id=?).
  • Privilege escalation: user sets role=admin in a PATCH body. Fix: allowlist writable fields.
  • CSRF for cookie auth: SameSite=Lax plus CSRF token on state-changing requests.
  • Session fixation, credential stuffing (rate limit + MFA), token theft via XSS (HttpOnly, CSP).
  • Confused deputy between services: pass the end user identity (token exchange, RFC 8693), do not trust a service-wide key for everything.
  • MFA: TOTP, push, or passkeys / WebAuthn (phishing-resistant, public-key per site).

Worked example. Breach pattern (Optus 2022 style): an unauthenticated API returned customer records by sequential id. Fix: auth on every endpoint, authz scoped by owner, non-guessable ids, rate limit enumeration (alert on 10k distinct ids per key per minute).

Industry examples. Facebook's 2018 "View As" token bug exposed 50M access tokens; Uber and Snapchat have had IDOR bugs. Service meshes (Istio, Linkerd) give mTLS identities so service-to-service authn is automatic.

Decision gravity. Enforcement in a shared middleware or library is cheap and reversible; scattering ad-hoc checks is how bugs happen. Making deny-by-default the default is a decision to take on day one.

Everyday analogy. A building with a lobby guard and also locks on every office door, because someone can always get past the lobby.

Common interview traps.

  • Trusting a user_id field in the request body.
  • Relying only on the gateway.
  • Skipping audit logs of authz decisions (needed for incident response).

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Authn = who; authz = what. Return 401 vs 403 correctly. Check object-level access on every request.
  • Store passwords as argon2id (or bcrypt) with unique salts; prefer passkeys and OIDC to avoid owning passwords.
  • Sessions: opaque id in an HttpOnly Secure SameSite cookie, Redis store, instant revoke. JWT: signed claims, local verification, no revoke before expiry.
  • Hybrid is typical: short access JWT (5 to 15 min) plus rotating opaque refresh token with reuse detection.
  • OAuth2 = delegated authorization (code flow + PKCE; client credentials for machines). OIDC adds the ID token for login; key users by iss + sub.
  • Revocation: short TTL, jti denylist, per-user valid_after, or introspection.
  • RBAC first; ABAC/ReBAC (OPA, Cedar, Zanzibar, SpiceDB) when roles explode or sharing graphs appear. Fail closed.
  • Authenticate at the edge, authorize in every service; deny by default; watch IDOR, privilege escalation, CSRF, XSS token theft.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between authentication and authorization, and which HTTP status codes map to each?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Candidates who blur the two ship IDOR bugs. This is the baseline vocabulary for every security discussion.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Authentication is "who are you", done once per login or token. Authorization is "what may you do to this resource", done on every request. Not authenticated is 401, authenticated but not allowed is 403. Authz must be checked per object, not just per endpoint.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Authn turns a credential (password, passkey, signed token) into an identity (user id, tenant, roles). Authz takes (identity, action, resource) and returns allow or deny.

Request -> [authn: who? -> identity] -> [authz: identity + action + resource?] -> handler
              401 if missing/invalid         403 if denied (or 404 to hide existence)

Authn is expensive and rare (argon2id about 100 ms per login). Authz is cheap and constant (microseconds, on in-memory claims or a cached policy). At 20M requests/day (about 230/s) you cannot afford a DB hit per authz check, so claims ride in the token or a cache.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
(object-level check, the part people forget) Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
Invoice inv = repo.findById(id).orElseThrow(NotFound::new);
if (!inv.getOwnerId().equals(principal.userId())) {
    throw new NotFound(); // 404 not 403: do not confirm the id exists
}
val inv = repo.findById(id) ?: throw NotFound()
if (inv.ownerId != principal.userId) throw NotFound() // hide existence

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using 401 for "forbidden" (clients then retry login in a loop).
  • Role check only in the UI or only at the gateway.
  • Endpoint-level check without object-level check (IDOR).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. 401 or 403 when the user is logged in but lacks the role? -> 403.
  2. Why sometimes return 404 instead of 403? -> To avoid leaking that the resource exists.
  3. Where do you enforce authz in microservices? -> At each service (defence in depth); the gateway only does coarse checks.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: definitions and status codes. Senior: object-level enforcement in every service, the cost asymmetry (rare expensive authn, constant cheap authz) and the 404-to-hide trade-off.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Most real breaches in this area are broken object-level authorization: the endpoint required login, but never checked that the invoice belonged to the caller.

questions.promptHtml: How should a system store user passwords, and why not SHA-256 or encryption?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you know that password hashing must be deliberately slow and salted, and what a database leak costs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Store a per-user salted hash from a slow, memory-hard function: argon2id, or bcrypt/scrypt if that is what the platform has. Never plain SHA-256 (too fast to brute-force) and never reversible encryption (a key leak exposes all). Optionally add a pepper held outside the DB.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A GPU does billions of SHA-256 per second, so a leaked fast-hash table falls to dictionary attacks in hours. Argon2id is tuned so one hash costs about 100 ms and tens of MB of RAM, which makes each guess expensive for the attacker too. A unique random salt per user defeats rainbow tables and makes identical passwords hash differently. A pepper (a secret from a vault or HSM, not in the DB) means a DB-only leak is not enough to crack offline.

Capacity: 1M logins/day = 12/s average, peak 3x = 36/s. At 100 ms CPU each that is about 3.6 cores at peak, so size login nodes for it and rate limit login, or the hash itself becomes your DoS vector.

Rehash on login lets you migrate parameters or algorithms: verify with the old scheme, then store with the new.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
from argon2 import PasswordHasher
ph = PasswordHasher(time_cost=3, memory_cost=64*1024, parallelism=2)  # tune to ~100 ms
h = ph.hash(password)           # salt generated and embedded in the string
ph.verify(h, attempt)           # raises on mismatch
if ph.check_needs_rehash(h):    # upgrade params at next login
    store(ph.hash(attempt))

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "I encrypt passwords with AES": reversible, one key leak ends it.
  • Global static salt, or salt equal to username.
  • Hashing on the client only (the hash becomes the password).
  • Unbounded password length (hash DoS): cap at a few hundred bytes.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Salt vs pepper? -> Salt is per-user, stored with the hash; pepper is one secret kept outside the DB.
  2. How to migrate from MD5 hashes? -> Wrap: argon2(md5hash) now, replace with argon2(password) at next login.
  3. How do you keep login from being a DoS vector? -> Per-IP and per-account rate limits, bounded concurrency on the hash pool, optionally a proof-of-work or captcha step.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "use bcrypt". Senior: tuned argon2id parameters from a latency budget, capacity math, pepper, rehash-on-login migration, and the DoS angle.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Breaches where passwords were unsalted SHA-1 got cracked at scale within days, leading to credential stuffing on other sites.

questions.contextHtml: You are designing auth for a B2C app: web, iOS and Android, 5M DAU, 40 requests per user per day (about 2,300/s average, 7k/s peak). Product asks for "ban a abusive user within 30 seconds" and "keep users logged in for 30 days". A teammate wants stateless JWTs with a 30-day expiry because "no session store, no scaling problem". Another wants server-side sessions in Redis.
questions.promptHtml: Which do you choose, and what is the decision gravity?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Picks JWT because "it scales" and never reconciles a 30-day token with a 30-second ban. Or picks sessions and ignores mobile/cross-service needs.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are there many backend services verifying identity, or one monolith? (JWT helps with many.) Is 30 s ban a hard SLO? What is the failure tolerance if the session store is down? Do third parties need tokens (OAuth)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; I give the numbers first. 7k/s peak against Redis is trivial (about 100k ops/s per node); statelessness is not buying scale here.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) opaque session id plus Redis: instant revoke, simple. (b) JWT access token with 5-minute expiry plus a rotating refresh token in the DB: stateless verification at services, revoke by refresh token and a small denylist. (c) pure 30-day JWT: cannot meet the ban SLO.
  4. How I'd verify: Load test a Redis replica set at 10k reads/s (expect sub-ms p99); measure token verify cost (about 50 us for ES256 verify, verify).
  5. Root cause of the dilemma: Stateless means no server memory to delete, so revocation needs either short TTL or a lookup.
  6. Fix: I pick (b) if there are many services and mobile clients: 5-minute JWT, 30-day rotating refresh token stored hashed in DB, a revocation list checked only for the ban path. If it is a single backend, plain sessions in Redis win on simplicity.
  7. Prevention: Alert on refresh failures and reuse detection hits; test the ban path end to end in staging.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use a 30-day access JWT. Token format is a two-way door early but gets one-way once mobile apps hold tokens, so decide before launch.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Redis goes down? -> Sessions: users logged out or fail closed; run replicated with persistence and a fallback read replica. JWT path keeps working for 5 minutes.
  • Where do you store the token on web? -> HttpOnly Secure SameSite cookie, not localStorage.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team shipped 24-hour JWTs, then a compromised account kept posting for a day because nothing could revoke it. They added a denylist keyed by jti, which quietly turned the stateless design into a stateful one.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "JWT scales, sessions don't".
  • Hire: Notes the revocation conflict and picks short-lived access plus refresh.
  • Strong hire: Uses the numbers to show a session store is cheap, ties choice to service count and client types, and names the one-way-door timing.

questions.contextHtml:
A code review shows this token check in an API gateway filter. The service handles money movement.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
public Claims authenticate(String token) {
    DecodedJWT jwt = JWT.decode(token);          // parses only
    if (jwt.getExpiresAt().before(new Date())) {
        throw new Unauthorized();
    }
    return jwt.getClaims();
}
fun authenticate(token: String): Map<String, Claim> {
    val jwt = JWT.decode(token)                  // parses only
    if (jwt.expiresAt.before(Date())) throw Unauthorized()
    return jwt.claims
}
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong, how would an attacker exploit it, and what is the corrected check?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Looks fine, it checks expiry." Misses that decode does not verify the signature.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which library and version? Which algorithm do we issue (HS256 vs RS256/ES256)? Do we use kid and a JWKS?
  2. Immediate mitigation: If this is live, it is critical: anyone can forge a token. Hotfix and consider rotating signing keys and invalidating sessions.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) no signature verification (the bug here); (2) missing iss and aud checks; (3) algorithm confusion (alg: none, or RS256 key used as HS256 secret); (4) no clock skew leeway.
  4. How I'd verify: Forge a token with {"sub":"admin"}, any signature, a far-future exp, and send it. If 200, confirmed.
  5. Root cause: JWT.decode is a base64 parser. A JWT is only trustworthy after verifying the signature with a key the server chose, not the one named in the header.
  6. Fix:
Algorithm alg = Algorithm.ECDSA256(publicKeyProvider);   // server-pinned algorithm
JWTVerifier v = JWT.require(alg)
    .withIssuer("https://auth.example.com")
    .withAudience("payments-api")
    .acceptLeeway(30)                                     // clock skew seconds
    .build();
DecodedJWT jwt = v.verify(token);                         // signature, exp, nbf, iss, aud
  1. Prevention: A test that sends an unsigned and a wrong-key token and expects 401; use a shared auth library instead of per-service parsing; a lint rule banning JWT.decode outside tests.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not trust the alg header, and I would not keep HS256 across many services (every verifier can mint tokens). Prefer asymmetric keys so services hold only the public key.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why are claims in the token not secret? -> They are only signed, base64-encoded, so never put PII or secrets there.
  • Key rotation? -> Publish a JWKS, use kid, keep the old key for the token TTL.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A service decoded the token for "logging convenience" and later reused the same decoded object for authorization; nobody noticed until a pen test forged an admin token.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Does not spot the missing verify.
  • Hire: Spots it, writes verification with expiry.
  • Strong hire: Adds issuer/audience, algorithm pinning, key rotation via kid, and a regression test.

questions.contextHtml:
A web app with 2M active sessions stores them in a single Redis node (maxmemory 8 GB, policy allkeys-lru). At 14:02 an unrelated team deploys a cache feature that fills the same Redis. Support gets 4,000 tickets in 20 minutes: "I was logged out". Metrics:

redis_evicted_keys_total      0 -> 9,800/s from 14:02
used_memory                   7.99 GB / 8 GB
session lookup miss rate      0.1% -> 38%
login endpoint QPS            150/s -> 2,900/s
argon2 CPU                    30% -> 100%, login p99 12 s
questions.promptHtml: Walk me through diagnosis, mitigation and the permanent fix.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Scale Redis up." Ignores that sessions and cache share one eviction policy and that the login stampede is a second outage.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the session store shared with cache? What is the eviction policy? Is there a login rate limit? Did a deploy happen?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Roll back the cache feature; raise maxmemory if the host has headroom. Cap login concurrency or rate limit it so the hashing pool does not melt; shed load with a friendly 503 and Retry-After. Do not restart Redis (it would drop all sessions).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) eviction of session keys by allkeys-lru because of shared memory (matches evicted keys spike); (2) a failover (no, no restart logs); (3) TTL misconfig (no, misses started at the deploy).
  4. How I'd verify: INFO memory, INFO stats (evicted_keys), redis-cli --bigkeys, MEMORY USAGE on the new key prefix, compare deploy time.
  5. Root cause: Sessions are state you cannot lose, but they shared a cache-grade eviction policy. When the cache grew, LRU evicted session keys, users got logged out and then stampeded the expensive login path.
  6. Fix: Short term: remove the cache feature, rate-limit login. Long term: separate Redis for sessions with noeviction (or volatile-ttl with only session keys), memory alarm at 70%, persistence (AOF everysec) and a replica.
  7. Prevention: Alert on evicted_keys > 0 for the session cluster, capacity review per keyspace, budget the hash pool and rate-limit login.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: noeviction means writes fail at full memory, so alert early. I would not move sessions to a DB just for this; a dedicated Redis is enough.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why 2,900 logins/s hurt so much? -> argon2 costs about 100 ms CPU; 2,900/s needs about 290 cores.
  • Could JWT avoid this? -> Yes for reads, but then you need a denylist for revocation.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A shared Redis "for everything" lost sessions every time a batch job ran; the fix was cheap, three separate instances by durability class.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Scales memory only.
  • Hire: Finds shared eviction and separates stores.
  • Strong hire: Also protects the login path from the stampede and adds eviction alerts.

questions.contextHtml:
A single-page app adds "Sign in with Google". A reviewer finds this config and flow:

oauth_client:
  response_type: token          # implicit flow, token returned in URL fragment
  redirect_uris:
    - https://*.example.com/callback
  state: null
  scopes: [openid, email, profile, drive]

The app never sends a state parameter, stores the access token in localStorage, and the product only needs the user's email.
questions.promptHtml: List what is wrong and what flow you would use instead.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Says "OAuth is fine because Google handles security". Misses wildcard redirect, no state, implicit flow and over-broad scope.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is there a backend we control (a BFF)? Does it need to call Drive at all? Which subdomains are user-controlled?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pin exact redirect URIs now; remove drive scope.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) wildcard redirect lets an attacker on any subdomain or open redirect capture the code/token; (2) missing state means login CSRF (attacker logs victim into attacker's account); (3) implicit flow leaks tokens in history and referrers; (4) least privilege violated by drive; (5) token in localStorage is stealable by any XSS.
  4. How I'd verify: Try authorizing with a redirect to evil.example.com (wildcard accepts); replay a callback without state.
  5. Root cause: Treating OAuth as a login checkbox rather than a protocol whose security comes from redirect-URI exactness, a bound state, and PKCE.
  6. Fix: Authorization code flow with PKCE (code_verifier and S256 challenge), exact-match redirect URI, random per-session state verified on callback, scopes openid email only, and prefer a backend-for-frontend that holds tokens and sets an HttpOnly session cookie.
  7. Prevention: Config linting in CI for wildcard URIs, security review of scopes, pen-test checklist for OAuth.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: BFF adds a server hop but removes tokens from the browser. I would not keep implicit flow for compatibility; it is deprecated.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What does PKCE protect against? -> A stolen authorization code being redeemed by someone without the verifier.
  • OAuth vs OIDC for login? -> OAuth grants access; OIDC adds an ID token to say who logged in.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A wildcard redirect plus an open-redirect page on a marketing subdomain let an attacker harvest codes from a phishing link that looked entirely legitimate.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Sees nothing wrong.
  • Hire: Fixes redirect, state, flow.
  • Strong hire: Adds PKCE, BFF, least privilege and CI linting.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect, and what are the ID token, access token and refresh token each for?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Using an access token as proof of identity is a classic design error.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: OAuth 2.0 is delegated authorization: it gives a client an access token to call an API on the user's behalf. OIDC is an identity layer on top that adds an ID token (a signed JWT saying who logged in, for the client) and a userinfo endpoint. Access token is for the resource server, ID token is for the client, refresh token gets new access tokens.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
User -> Client -> Authorization server (login + consent)
Client <- code -> Client exchanges code (+PKCE verifier) at token endpoint
Client <- { access_token, id_token, refresh_token }
Client -> Resource API with access_token (Bearer)
  • ID token: audience is the client id; contains sub, iss, aud, exp, nonce. The client validates it. It is never sent to APIs.
  • Access token: audience is the API; opaque or JWT. The API validates scope and audience.
  • Refresh token: long-lived, held confidentially, exchanged for new access tokens; rotate it.
  • nonce ties the ID token to the login request (replay defence), state ties the callback to the browser session.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Treating a valid access token as proof the user is present and logging in with it.
  • Sending the ID token to the API as a bearer credential.
  • Not validating aud and iss.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why the authorization code flow and not implicit? -> Tokens come over a back channel, not the browser URL.
  2. What is the sub claim good for? -> A stable per-issuer user id; never key accounts on email alone.
  3. Machine-to-machine? -> Client credentials grant, no user, no ID token.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "OIDC is OAuth plus login". Senior: names which token goes where, audience validation, nonce vs state, and account linking pitfalls on email.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An app accepted any Google access token as login; a token issued to a different app could be replayed to impersonate users.

questions.contextHtml:
Mobile app, access token 10 minutes, refresh token 60 days, non-rotating, stored in plain app storage. Security notices a surge:

auth-service log, one refresh token (rt_9f..a1):
10:01:04 refresh ok  ip=49.x.x.12  device=Pixel-7
10:01:09 refresh ok  ip=185.x.x.88 device=unknown  ua=python-requests
10:07:11 refresh ok  ip=185.x.x.88
...
185.x.x.88 shows 1,100 refreshes in 6 hours across 340 distinct tokens
questions.promptHtml: What happened, what do you do now, and how do you redesign refresh?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Just blocks the IP. The tokens are still valid and the next IP works.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How were tokens stored? Was there a malicious SDK or leaked backup? Are tokens bound to a device?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Revoke all 340 tokens and their token families, force re-login for affected users, block the IP as a stopgap, and notify users.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) refresh tokens exfiltrated from device storage or a log; (2) leaked from a server log or analytics payload; (3) credential stuffing (no, tokens not passwords).
  4. How I'd verify: Search logs/crash reports for rt_ strings, check which app versions and OS the 340 users share, correlate with a third-party SDK release.
  5. Root cause: Non-rotating bearer refresh tokens are as good as passwords for 60 days; a copy is indistinguishable from the original.
  6. Fix: Rotating refresh tokens with reuse detection. Each refresh issues a new token and invalidates the old; if an old one is presented, revoke the whole family.
family f1: rt1 -> rt2 -> rt3
attacker presents rt1 after rt2 exists  => reuse detected => revoke f1, force login

Store tokens in Keychain/Keystore, bind to device key where possible (DPoP, verify), hash tokens in the DB, absolute lifetime cap. 7. Prevention: Alert on refresh from two ASNs inside minutes; never log tokens; add a grace window of a few seconds so a retry after a network blip does not nuke a family. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Reuse detection logs out honest users after flaky networks if there is no grace window. I would not shorten to 5 minutes alone; the thief refreshes anyway.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Two tabs refresh at once? -> Serialize refresh client-side or accept the grace window.
  • What if the family is huge? -> Index by family id; revoke by one write.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A logging library captured request bodies, refresh tokens included, into a searchable index that three vendors could read.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Blocks the IP only.
  • Hire: Revokes and proposes rotation.
  • Strong hire: Reuse detection with family revocation, grace window, storage hardening and a leak investigation.

questions.contextHtml: A platform with 20M MAU uses 15-minute JWT access tokens, verified locally by 60 services. Security now requires "logout everywhere, account compromise lock, and employee offboarding take effect in under 10 seconds". Peak 50k requests/s across services. A proposal: every service calls the auth service to validate each token. Another: a denylist in Redis.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Central validation of every request (50k/s extra hops, new single point of failure) or "just make tokens 10 seconds".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is 10 s needed for all users or only high-risk events? What is the fail-open policy if the revocation source is down? How many revocations per day?
  2. Immediate mitigation: For the very high-risk cases (compromise, offboarding) push a revocation event now; for the rest let the 15-minute TTL absorb it.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) per-token denylist (jti) in Redis, size = revocations in the last 15 min only; (b) per-user "not before" timestamp (tokens_valid_after), one small key per revoked user; (c) central introspection per call; (d) 10-second tokens.
  4. How I'd verify: Size it: say 200k revocations/day, peak 5k per 15 min; a denylist of 5k entries is a few hundred KB, fits in every service's memory.
  5. Root cause: Stateless verification has no way to learn about events after issue; the only choices are expiry or pushing state to verifiers.
  6. Fix: Chosen design (b): store valid_after[user] and push changes over pub/sub (Redis or Kafka) to every service's in-memory map, with a Redis read fallback on a miss. Verification becomes: signature OK, iat >= valid_after[user]. Entries expire after 15 minutes. Services check locally in nanoseconds; propagation is about 1 s.
  7. Prevention: Measure propagation lag as an SLO; chaos test with the bus down: high-risk endpoints fail closed, low-risk fail open to TTL.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not introspect every call (50k/s of extra latency and a new SPOF) and would not drop to 10 s tokens (refresh traffic of 20M x 6/min is absurd). The cost is eventual consistency of about a second.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Bus partition? -> Services fall back to TTL; high-risk actions (payments) re-check live.
  • Single token revoke? -> jti denylist alongside valid_after.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A fired contractor's token worked for 55 minutes because "revocation" meant waiting for expiry; the postmortem added the pushed valid_after map.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Central call per request.
  • Hire: Denylist with TTL equal to token life.
  • Strong hire: Sizes the data, pushes to memory, defines fail-open/closed per risk class.

questions.promptHtml: Compare RBAC, ABAC and relationship-based access control. When would you use each, and how do you make the decision at scale?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Senior engineers must choose an authorization model that will not collapse under new requirements.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: RBAC grants permissions to roles, simple and auditable but it explodes with fine-grained or per-object rules. ABAC evaluates attributes of user, resource and context against policy, flexible but harder to reason about. ReBAC (Zanzibar style) derives access from relationships like "member of group that owns folder", ideal for sharing graphs like Docs or Drive. Most systems start with RBAC and add attributes or relations where needed.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
RBAC : user -> role -> permission               (admin can delete)
ABAC : allow if user.dept == doc.dept AND time in office hours AND doc.classification <= user.clearance
ReBAC: doc:42#viewer@user:alice  via  folder:7#parent, group:eng#member
  • RBAC check is a set lookup, cacheable. Fails when roles multiply (role explosion: editor-eu-finance-readonly).
  • ABAC needs a policy engine (OPA, Cedar) and clear attribute sources; testing and explaining "why denied" matter.
  • ReBAC stores tuples and answers "does a path exist from user to object" with graph expansion plus caching and consistency tokens ("zookies") to avoid the new-enemy problem. Scale: 10M objects with 5 sharing relations each is about 50M tuples; checks need caching and often a dedicated service.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Building RBAC for a sharing product with per-document grants.
  • ABAC policies nobody can audit.
  • Remote policy call on every request without caching or a local fallback.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you list "all docs Alice can view"? -> Reverse expansion, or pre-computed index; it is harder than the point check.
  2. Where does policy live? -> Central engine with local sidecar caching, policies versioned and tested.
  3. What is the new-enemy problem? -> Removing access then adding content must not let the removed user see it; consistency tokens bound staleness.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: define the three. Senior: ties model to product shape, handles list queries, caching, consistency and auditability.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A document app started with three roles, then needed per-link sharing; the bolt-on ACL table and the role code disagreed and leaked docs.

questions.contextHtml:
A B2B SaaS has 3,000 tenants. Every customer asked for custom permissions, so engineering created roles per request. Now there are 410 roles, 1,900 role-permission rows per tenant on average, and a permission check query joins 4 tables:

SELECT 1 FROM user_roles ur JOIN role_perms rp ON ... JOIN perms p ON ... WHERE ur.user_id=? AND p.name=?
authz p99: 4 ms -> 38 ms at 12k checks/s peak; DB CPU 70%
support: "Why can Maria delete invoices?" takes an hour to answer

You want to restructure without downtime.
questions.promptHtml: How do you fix the model and migrate it live?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add an index and a cache." Treats it as a performance bug rather than a model problem, and proposes a big-bang rewrite.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which roles differ materially vs duplicates? Is the custom need per-tenant or per-resource? Who audits access (compliance)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cache the resolved permission set per (tenant, user) with a 60 s TTL, invalidated on role change; this removes most of the 12k/s DB hits.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) roles are mostly bundles of a small permission vocabulary (about 60 permissions); (2) some "roles" are really attributes (region, department) that RBAC cannot express; (3) a few need resource-level rules.
  4. How I'd verify: Cluster roles by permission set (Jaccard similarity); expect 410 to collapse to around 15 canonical roles plus per-tenant overrides.
  5. Root cause: Using roles for every distinction. Roles should represent job functions; scoping (region, owner) belongs in attributes or resource relations.
  6. Fix: Fewer base roles plus scoped grants (role, scope) and attribute rules for the few cases, with a single can(user, action, resource) function behind an interface. Migrate by: (a) build new engine, (b) shadow mode: evaluate both, log diffs (should be zero), (c) fix diffs, (d) flip per-tenant via flag, (e) delete old tables later. Compile effective permissions into a denormalised table or token claims for fast checks.
  7. Prevention: Policy as code in review; an "explain" endpoint; quarterly role review; limit custom roles per tenant.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Denormalised permissions need invalidation on change; accept up to 60 s staleness except for removals (push those). I would not rewrite everything at once nor delete the old model before shadow diffs hit zero.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Shadow diffs show 2%? -> Inspect: usually inherited default roles or legacy rows; fix data before the flip.
  • Tenant wants custom roles still? -> Allow composition of the small permission vocabulary, not new code paths.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A shadow-mode diff found 11 users with delete rights nobody could explain; the cleanup was a bigger win than the speedup.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Index and cache only.
  • Hire: Role consolidation plus staged migration.
  • Strong hire: Shadow mode with diffs, scoped grants, explainability and caching with removal-push semantics.

questions.contextHtml: Post-incident review. An attacker with a free account called GET /api/orders/{id} on the order service by iterating ids and downloaded 41,000 orders of other customers over three days (about 1 request/s, so no rate alarm). The API gateway validated the JWT and checked the orders:read scope. The order service "trusts the gateway" and loads any order by id. The attacker also reached the order service directly through a mistakenly public load balancer, bypassing the gateway.
questions.promptHtml: Run the post-incident review: root causes, fixes, and detection.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add rate limiting." Treats the symptom; leaves the missing object check and the trust model.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Were ids sequential? Which identity headers does the order service accept? Which networks can reach it? How long were logs kept?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Close the public LB, add the ownership check as a hotfix, rotate any exposed credentials, preserve logs, begin breach assessment and notification obligations with legal.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) broken object-level authorization (IDOR); (2) gateway-only enforcement with implicit trust; (3) predictable sequential ids; (4) network exposure; (5) no anomaly detection (red herring: scope check was fine).
  4. How I'd verify: Query access logs: one user id touching 41k distinct order ids owned by others; compare order.customer_id != token.sub counts.
  5. Root cause: Authorization was coarse (scope) and enforced in one place. Nothing asked "does this order belong to this caller".
  6. Fix: Check order.tenant/customer == principal in the service (or add WHERE customer_id = :sub to every query), pass a verified identity (signed token or mTLS-bound), non-guessable ids (UUIDv4/v7 as defence in depth, not a fix), private network only plus mTLS between services.
  7. Prevention: Authorization tests per endpoint (user A reading user B's object must 404), a shared authz library, scan for "findById without owner filter", alert on one principal reading many distinct objects, automated exposure scans of LBs.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Per-service checks add duplicated logic; mitigate with a common library and policy engine. I would not rely on UUIDs alone, and not on the gateway alone.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Gateway needs to pass user id downstream? -> Signed internal token, never a plain X-User-Id header trusted from the network.
  • How to find other affected endpoints? -> Audit every route taking an object id and add the test.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: The fix PR was three lines; the review of the other 140 endpoints found nine more of the same bug.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Rate limiting.
  • Hire: Object-level check and network closure.
  • Strong hire: Layered enforcement, identity propagation, tests, detection of low-and-slow enumeration and breach handling.
